Why Is Everyone So Obsessed With Protein?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Gut Check, our column dedicated to the complex, ever-evolving relationship between food and our bodies.
  • I recently shed 20 pounds for my health, and I’m keeping it off by avoiding simple carbohydrates—pasta, pastries, white rice, most breads—and exercising with weights and resistance bands.
  • Sources indicate that in my current obsession with protein, I’m not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Gut Check, our column dedicated to the complex, ever-evolving relationship between food and our bodies. Whether you’re curious about mindful eating or want to understand what makes picky eaters picky, read on and let award-winning journalist Betsy Andrews answer all your burning questions.

I recently shed 20 pounds for my health, and I’m keeping it off by avoiding simple carbohydrates—pasta, pastries, white rice, most breads—and exercising with weights and resistance bands. Carbs make you feel full, at least temporarily, and without them, especially when I’m hungry after a workout, I’m turning to an even more filling macronutrient: protein. I’m 63, and my wife is 60. We’ve heard that dietary protein is key to wellness in aging. But, after recent blood work, she is worrying about “bad,” or LDL, cholesterol. All this leaves me pondering the types and amounts of proteins I should be cooking that won’t increase her cholesterol levels or my waistline but will make for satisfying, healthy meals.

Sources indicate that in my current obsession with protein, I’m not alone. Americans are bingeing on the stuff: Social media is glutted with influencers promoting protein powders and heavy meat consumption; supermarket shelves have filled with packaged snacks advertising excess protein; and restaurants are overhauling menus to feed the needs of protein-hungry diners. Even the latest USDA dietary guidelines encourage protein uptake. At its extreme, it’s a trend known as protein-maxxing, and everyone from the Kardashians to the American Medical Association is talking about it.

Industry observers note that our bodies need protein to function. “Protein is made of amino acids. When we digest protein, we release those amino acids and use them to build and maintain our own proteins: muscle, liver, heart, lungs, and even some bone,” explains kinesiology professor Stuart Phillips, director of the Physical Activity Centre of Excellence (PACE) at Ontario’s McMaster University in Canada. “Protein supplies materials for enzymes, antibodies, transport proteins, some hormones, and the repair of tissues and organs.”.

It has been revealed that of the 20 amino acids in our bodies, nine are essential, meaning we can’t create them ourselves. We must get them from eating protein, and we need to keep up protein consumption, because our bodies deplete it as we digest it. “The simple takeaway is that protein builds you from the inside out. It is foundational,” says dietitian Daphene Altema-Johnson, senior program officer at the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future. “But unlike fat, your body doesn’t have a dedicated storage system for protein, so you need a steady supply from food.”.

In a culture built on body image, protein is also touted for its body-sculpting and weight-loss benefits. “You use protein to help build and maintain muscle mass and also recover from a workout,” explains Zach Rocheleau, the creator of the protein-rich recipes that comprise The Flexible Dieting Lifestyle. “It’s also the most satiating macronutrient. Getting the satiety effects of protein and thus feeling full, so eating less calories, is the driver that goes into losing weight.”.

When influencers like Rocheleau claim that the protein they’re eating has helped them shape their physique, they aren’t wrong. Research does show that if you eat more protein it assists (to a point) in building lean muscle mass during resistance training. And studies have established the relationship between protein consumption, satiation, and weight loss. “The hype has come from real physiological needs,” indicates Dr. Megan Rossi, founder of The Gut Health Doctor, “but it’s more of an aesthetic effect, where people associate protein with big muscles and think the more protein they eat, the bulkier they’ll get.”.

In a recent development, scarfing down cheeseburgers and looking great doing it sounds good, but eating too much protein can put stress on your body, especially the kidneys. When you eat protein, Altema-Johnson explains, “The nitrogen part of it is stripped off and converted to urea, which is filtered out by your kidneys. Lots of nitrogen waste leads to a chronically higher kidney workload.”.

For most people, this shouldn’t be much to worry about: Though he notes that this isn’t an endorsement of long-term protein bingeing, Phillips’ meta-analysis found no negative effect of higher protein consumption on kidney function in healthy adults. But if your kidneys aren’t in tip-top shape, stressing them can contribute to high blood pressure and other heart conditions. And studies show that consume excess animal-based proteins, in particular, can increase the risk of kidney stones.

In a recent development, there’s another potential problem: Your small intestine can only digest so much protein, so in high amounts, some of it ends up in your colon, where it can produce potentially harmful by-products. “Excess protein, like poorly absorbed egg whites and red meat, can ferment and produce toxic metabolites, which are associated with heart disease,” states Rossi. The solution is to eat fiber as well. But when you’re protein-maxxing, other nutrients, including fiber, can fall to the wayside.

In a recent development, finally, though protein-maxxing is often touted as a way to slim down, the opposite can be true, too. “Your body has a ceiling for how much protein you can use,” notes Altema-Johnson. Excess protein gets converted into glucose or fat for energy. Calories are energy units. You only need so many of them, and if you’re “chasing a protein number instead of eating until full,” as Altema-Johnson puts it, studies show that the extra calories can lead to weight gain.

According to recent reports, some protein-enriched packaged foods harbor sneaky calories. According to Rocheleau—who, by the way, eschews the phrase “protein-maxxing” in his work—“You would think that somebody putting out a high-protein product would take calories from carbs and fats and replace them with protein, but generally they keep the product the same but add protein, so you’re getting a lot more calories.” Plus, the marketing of protein-added snacks actually creates an insidious halo effect. “If you slap ‘high protein’ on a package, there’s the perception that it is automatically healthy, which can lead to overconsumption,” says Altema-Johnson. And while dairy- or plant-based protein products, including powdered supplements, can be a convenient way to support higher training needs to fill a genuine gap in the diet, Phillips’ research demonstrates that they’re not a substitute for exercise itself and that protein intake had diminishing gains over a certain amount.

So what is the optimum amount of protein we should consume? Guidelines differ. Like the USDA previously, Canadian guidelines suggest a daily protein intake of .8 grams per kilogram of body weight. (To convert your body weight from pounds to kilograms, just divide it by 2.2.) For me, at 77 kilograms, 62 grams of protein per day is a good target, according to these guidelines, which comes out to a little over 8 ounces of roast chicken to meet my goals for the day. U.K. guidelines recommend slightly less, at .75 grams per kilogram, while the latest USDA guidelines have been cranked up to 1.2 to 1.6 grams. At that serving goal, I can scarf down more than a pound of roast bird a day, and in theory, that’s what experts want me to do. For active and older adults, Phillips likes the new USDA targets, because we lose muscle mass as we age, and we start to need more protein to help retain it.

But not all protein is created equal. With my partner’s concern over cholesterol, maybe a skin-on bird dripping fat or a well-marbled steak seared in butter, both high in saturated fat, isn’t optimal for us. “This is where individualization matters,” states Altema-Johnson. “The goal is not zero red meat, but smaller proportions, moderation, and smarter cuts.” Experts like her, and plenty of studies, will warn you away from fattier and, especially, processed meats. “Unprocessed steak, ground beef, even pork chops have a modest health-associated risk,” Altema-Johnson says. “But bacon, sausage, deli meat, hot dogs—if you’re eating those constantly, you’re at higher risk for heart disease, colorectal cancer, and other health concerns.”.

Recent findings suggest that unlike animal proteins, not all plants contain every amino acid that our bodies need. But you can combine various vegetable proteins to meet those goals. Phillips and his colleagues found that young vegan and omnivorous men eating around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day achieved similar muscle and strength gains with resistance training. “Grains tend to be relatively low in lysine. Legumes help address that limitation, while grains complement legumes’ amino acid profiles,” he says. “Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, edamame, eggs, milk, yogurt, nuts, and seeds can all contribute. Soy is a particularly useful plant protein.” You don’t have to mix and match them at every meal, but a diverse plant-based diet can bring the protein you need.

According to recent reports, the biggest takeaway is that you can’t just protein-max in the absence of overall healthy lifestyle choices. One of those is a balanced diet. According to Altema-Johnson, we should “individualize, moderate and balance. It’s important to have a diverse plate. If you’re focusing on one type of protein, especially meat, you’re missing out on all the good yummies a body needs.”.

Chief among those yummies is fiber. Rossi says that recent studies support the idea that increasing protein can have benefits for weight-lifting and even aging, “but you need to increase fiber to balance it so your microbiome has more to eat than just excess protein. We need to swing the fiber flag.” Another recent study revealed that 93 percent of Americans get enough protein, but other research reveals the opposite for fiber: Just 7 percent of us eat an adequate amount. That’s not good. A review of more than 5,000 studies found that a diet low in red meat but high in fiber-rich whole grains, vegetables, and nuts lowered our risk of death due to heart disease. “For gut health,” Phillips says, we should “ask what your protein habit is pushing off the plate.”.

Sources indicate that the other important lifestyle choice is exercise. “You can’t just expect to be sitting on the couch and eating protein and having these huge gains. Physical activity and resistance training bring far bigger results,” Rossi notes. That’s why I’ve ultimately been committed to moving more: Preventing muscle loss is insurance for my future. “Without enough protein and—most importantly, in my opinion—resistance exercise, this loss speeds up significantly,” says Altema-Johnson. “It affects strength, ability, balance, and fall risk. Muscle loss is directly tied to independence. It’s the difference between carrying your own groceries at 80 or needing help.”.

Industry observers note that of course, I’m getting a late start. “You do not wake up at 65 with a new protein requirement. Start paying attention in midlife (over 40), and pair the protein with strength training, as that is the big lever to promote health, not protein,” notes Phillips. Well, I’m not 65 yet, but I did almost hit that age without addressing these health needs. Now I know that I need to exercise, and to support the training, I need a bit more protein, but not piles of it, and it has to come from a variety of sources. Perhaps most importantly, I’ll continue to take whatever the trend-setters are pushing on the socials with a grain of salt. As Phillips puts it, “Protein is a nutrient, not an identity. The goal is enough to support health, not as much as you can eat.”.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

Industry observers note that the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., remarked in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler noted, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At glitch in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura noted his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

According to recent reports, jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He stated that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, remarked that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors stated he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely latest bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A upcoming Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

In a recent development, congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco mentioned he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

In a recent development, the House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a latest version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that highly-evolved stars spread the material for fresh planets and stars into space with their stellar winds.
  • The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind.
  • According to recent reports, researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that highly-evolved stars spread the material for fresh planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

According to recent reports, researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe.".

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

In a recent development, âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

In a recent development, this schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics.

In a recent development, astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

It has been revealed that recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

According to recent reports, this time-lapse demonstrates ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

Industry observers note that âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," stated study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

According to recent reports, some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

Industry observers note that but the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

In a recent development, âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

Sources indicate that âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That highlighted us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," stated Vlemmings.

According to recent reports, this figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

Recent findings suggest that for now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

Industry observers note that the flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a latest element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â remarked Andriantsaralaza.

This research shows that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

"The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

"Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," said Vlemmings.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.
  • The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument.
  • According to recent reports, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever fresh ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

According to recent reports, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever fresh ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

According to recent reports, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

Industry observers note that while more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Sources indicate that I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated promptly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

#226439. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1692 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI).
  • It has been revealed that today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century.
  • This era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our previous installments, we examined the inspiration and earliest experiments in this field. We then looked at how it co-evolved with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), leading to the first true attempt to send a message of greeting to the stars (the Arecibo Message). We followed up with a look at two of the brightest minds in the business (Frank Drake and Carl Sagan), the brains behind the first interstellar messages (the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records).

It has been revealed that today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century. And just like SETI, the number of experiments has grown considerably, thanks to renewed interest in space exploration following fresh efforts to explore Mars and the Solar System. This included the first orbital observatory, the venerable Hubble Space Telescope, and deep space probes like the Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Magellan, and Venus Express missions.

This era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars. These included orbiters like the Mars Odyssey and Mars Express missions, and rovers and landers like Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, as well as Spirit and Opportunity. These experiments also reflected the changing nature of space exploration, which included missions from emerging space agencies, non-profits, and private entities.

All of these experiments built on the legacy of the Arecibo Message, adding additional information and personal touches where the creators desired.

It has been revealed that an explanatory diagram of a message transmitted in 1983 by Masaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi to Altair. Credit: ShizuShizu/Wikimedia.

Recent findings suggest that in 1983, astronomers Masaaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi used the Stanford Dish radio telescope at Stanford University to transmit the Message to Altair (or the Call to the Cosmos 83'). The message was produced in collaboration with the Japanese publication Weekly Shonen Jump and transmitted on August 15th, 1983, to commemorate the publication's 15th anniversary. The destination was Altair, an A-type blue-white giant star located 16.7 light-years from Earth, which represents the Shinto deity Hikoboshi in the Tanabata legend.

Like the Arecibo Message, the content was a symbolic, graphic message meant to convey information about humanity, life on Earth, and peace. Unlike the Arecibo message, the Message to Altair consisted of several pages rather than a single, long pictograph, each dealing with a different subject. The first page included mathematical information, such as the numbers 1 to 12, prime numbers, powers of 3, formulas for indicating addition and multiplication, and chemical elements essential to life.

For this, Morimoto and Hirabayashi chose hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, the building blocks of stars and planetary systems. Several other molecules were included, including hydroxide, water, nitrous oxide, formaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and their respective wavelengths. All of these chemicals play a central role in prebiotic chemistry and the formation of organic molecules that give rise to life.

Industry observers note that page two included information on the Solar System, including (from top to bottom) the Sun, the planets in order of distance, some of the larger moons, and their equatorial radii and mean distances from the Sun. Pages three and four included the chemical formulae for DNA compounds, as well as showing DNA structure and replication. This was followed by a series of drawings that showed different types of life forms on Earth, and they were arranged to convey the process of biological evolution.

They begin with pictures of early primitive life, followed by jellyfish, fish, amphibians, lizards, early mammals, apes, and then humans. Like the Pioneer Plaques, this image indicates a man and a woman with two children between them. This was followed by a close-up illustration of the woman's face waving hello. The last page highlighted the transmission parameters: the total number of bits, the transmission wavelength, and the radius of the radio telescope that beamed the message.

It also contained the Japanese and English spelling for the word "toast," followed by the chemical formula for ethanol alcohol - in short, the message concludes with the raising of a toast with an alcoholic drink.

Industry observers note that the thirteen pictures that make up the Message to Altair, listed in order (left to right, top to bottom). Credit: Shinya Nurasawa.

As Altair is approximately 17 light-years distant, the message would have arrived around 2000, and the window for a reply would open by 2017. In 2023, Hyogo University astronomer Shin-ya Narusawa (who knew Morimoto before his death) asked the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to help search for a possible reply. JAXA obliged and used the radio antenna at the Usuda Space Observatory to observe Altair for an hour at 10 p.m. on August 22nd, 2023.

Sources indicate that the date was significant because it also fell on Tanabata in the old Japanese calendar and is the only day of the year when the deities Orihime and Hikoboshi (represented by Vega and Altair, respectively) are allowed to meet. The observations detected no signals, but Narusawa mentioned he intends to continue observing and collaborating with other research institutions.

Between 1999 and 2003, three METI experiments were conducted using the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR), a Soviet-era facility located in the Crimea for deep-space communications and radio astronomy. All four projects were organized with help from famed Soviet-Russian radio engineer, astronomer, and SETI researcher Alexander Zaitsev. As we addressed in part I of the series, he coined the term METI in his 2006 paper, Messaging to Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence.

According to recent reports, the first project to use the EPR RT-70 radio telescope was the Cosmic Call, which included two broadcasts, one sent in 1999 and the other in 2003. The venture was a crowdsourced effort by Texas-based startup Team Encounter, Canadian astrophysicist Yvan Dutil, Russian scientists (including Zaitsev), and Eastern European radio engineers.

The message included contributions by Dutil and his fellow physicist StÃ©phane Dumas. Their primer was inspired by Hans Freudenthal's 1960 book Lincos: Design of a Language for Cosmic Intercourse, which describes a language designed to be understandable to an extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI). Using Lincos, Dutil and Dumas' message (DDM) was carefully structured to include pictograms showing mathematics, physics (the hydrogen spectrum), and related concepts.

The second part consisted of a series of pictograms created by Richard Braastad of Team Encounter, the Braastad Message (DM). It used mathematical symbols to describe a solar sail (another project Team Encounter was working on), including its dimensions, payload, trajectory, and projected launch time. This was followed by the original Arecibo Message (AM), the company's Team Encounter 2001 Staff Message (ESM), and a message composed with input from the public - the Public Part (PP).

The second page of the primer prepared by Dutil and Dumas, denoting mathematical concepts (part of the Cosmic Call). Credit: Dumas, S.

According to recent reports, the broadcast was broken into four sessions, lasting a total of 40 hours, with each session targeting a different Sun-like (G-type) star system. These included 16 Cygni A on May 24th, 1999, a G-type star in a triple-star system located 69 light-years from Earth. On June 30th, 1999, the target was 15 Sagittae, another G-type star about 58 light-years from Earth in the Sagittarius Constellation. Lastly, and again on June 30th, 1999, the team transmitted to HD 178428, a G-type star located 69 light-years away, also in the Sagittarius Constellation.

Sources indicate that each session of Cosmic Call 1 transmitted the scientific parts (DDM, BM, AM, and ESM) three times at 100 bits per second, followed by the Public Part (PP), sent once at 2000 bits/s. The full message was structured as:.

DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â PP.

The second Cosmic Call, in 2003, followed a similar structure. For this message, Dutil and Dumas presented an updated version of their Lincos pictographs (DDM2), the Arecibo Message, the Bilingual Image Glossary, and the same Public Part. The structure was as follows:.

DDM2 â DDM2 â DDM2 â AM â AM â AM â BIG â BIG â BIG â BM â ESM â PP,.

The destinations for this message included five more stars, with all transmissions occurring on the same day (July 6th, 2033). They included GJ 49, a G-type star located 32 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia, on July 6th, 2003. This was followed by Gliese 208, an M-type (red dwarf) star 37 light-years away in the constellation Orion; 55 Cancri, an M-type star 41 light-years away in Cancer; HD 10307, a binary star system with a G-type primary and an M-type companion 42.6 light-years away in Andromeda; and 47 Ursae Majoris, a G-type star located 45.3 light-years away in Ursa Major.

According to recent reports, the Cosmic Calls were the most ambitious public SETI/METI effort mounted to date. While Team Encounter went bankrupt in the years that followed, their messages established a precedent that would be joined by several more METI efforts in the fresh millennium. Zaitsev would play a key role in several, and his work with his colleagues would culminate by 2008 in the creation of METI International. More on that soon!

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there are certain foods that we wish we could package up and save forever, and tomatoes are at the top of that list. Canning is an excellent way to hold onto the fleeting abundance of summer, when these versatile fruits are at their ripest, juiciest, and most flavorful. Canning may never be able to re-create the feeling of picking a plump, juicy tomato fresh from the vine and slicing it while it’s still warm from the sun, but in the depths of winter, we’ll take what we can get. Whether they are using diced, puréed, crushed, or whole canned tomatoes, these recipes make the most of the ingredient, extending its life well beyond the growing season.

Sources indicate that this classic sauce from Bolognese cooking teachers Margherita and Valeria Simili combines ground beef with prosciutto, chicken livers, milk, and tomato purée. The slow-simmered sauce is a natural partner for serving over pasta or as a hearty filling for lasagna. Get the recipe >.

Stalks of crisp celery are cut into bite-size pieces and slowly braised with tomatoes, onion, prosciutto, and olive oil until tender. This simple Italian preparation transforms a vegetable that’s often an afterthought into a comforting side dish. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, agrodolce, or “sour and sweet” in Italian, is a classic Sicilian sauce, here paired with tender steamed broccoli. Red wine, canned tomatoes, vinegar, raisins, and black olives give the sauce its characteristic sweet-tart and slightly salty balance, while toasted pine nuts add a little crunch. Get the recipe >.

In this simple recipe, beef short ribs slowly braise with red wine, garlic, onion, and canned tomatoes until the meat is fall-apart tender. It’s a hearty, straightforward one-pot meal that makes especially good use of pantry staples. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that this stuffed pasta with ridged edges from celebrated Los Angeles chef Evan Funke pairs a filling of ricotta and greens with a humble lightly cooked tomato sauce. Get the recipe >.

This classic Sicilian dish balances tender fried eggplant with caramelized onions, golden raisins, olives, capers, and a sweet-tart tomato sauce. An unexpected addition of unsweetened chocolate brings a subtle bitterness that rounds out the sweet and savory flavors. Get the recipe >.

While not the pizza that many people think of, this beloved Rhode Island specialty features thick, airy rectangles of focaccia-like dough topped with a simple tomato sauce. Traditionally served at room temperature, they’re a fixture at bakeries, parties, and family gatherings. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that lamb, torn pita, and herbs are formed into tender rounds and simmered in a spicy tomato sauce, then finished with a cool, lemony aioli. The dish can be prepared ahead and reheated before serving, with the greens and sauce added at the last minute. Get the recipe >.

Sources indicate that A tomato-packed broth made with topneck clams and salt pork provides the foundation for this hearty soup. The mixture is chilled overnight, giving the flavors time to meld before being finished with bacon, onion, celery, garlic, and fresh herbs. Get the recipe >.

Roasted pumpkin, winter squash, sweet potato, and bell pepper are folded into a tomato-based sauce spiced with cumin, coriander, and harissa. Chickpeas and dried apricots make the stew hearty and subtly sweet, while bulgur mixed with dried cherries and raisins makes for a flavorful, filling base. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that these crisp, golden fritters bring together tender Sea Island red peas, Carolina Gold rice, and collard greens in a nod to the flavors of South Carolina’s Lowcountry. The accompanying sauce simmers canned tomatoes with brown sugar, cider vinegar, and smoked paprika, creating a bright, tangy dip with just a hint of sweetness and smoke. Get the recipe >.

Recent findings suggest that this Sicilian baked pasta layers ring-shaped noodles with a tomato-rich ragù of beef, pork, and peas, plus fried eggplant, hard-boiled eggs, ham, and cheese. It’s the kind of deeply layered, all-in-one dish that makes for the perfect centerpiece when cooking for a crowd. Get the recipe >.

Sources indicate that this Roman classic gets its character from slow-braised oxtail and an unusually simple combination of tomatoes and celery, with no garlic or onions. The sauce is even better made a day or two ahead, giving the flavors time to deepen before it’s tossed with the cooked pasta. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, creamy polenta provides the filling backbone of this dish, while sausage stewed in marinara sauce brings a rich, savory depth. Finished with grated Pecorino Romano, it’s a classic Italian comfort food that’s hearty, satisfying, and perfect for a cozy dinner. Get the recipe >.

This cultural mash-up pairs chewy udon noodles with a deeply savory tomato sauce spiked with guanciale, white miso, chile, and Pecorino Romano. The sauce starts with canned San Marzano tomatoes, which simmer with garlic and onion until thick and rich. Get the recipe >.

This southern Italian dish from famed cookbook author Marcella Hazan pairs seared lamb chops with a simple skillet sauce of canned San Marzano tomatoes, sweet red peppers, green olives, onion, and parsley. The chops finish in the sauce, picking up its savory, briny flavor. Get the recipe >.

Fresh chiles are cooked alongside onions, garlic, and spices, providing an aromatic base for the sauce of crushed tomatoes. Eggs provide a hit of protein and a richness to counteract the sauce’s heat and acidity, while a sprinkling of feta cheese and chopped parsley add a touch of saltiness and verdant freshness. Get the recipe >.

A year-round take on a classic Italian summer salad, this version uses canned tomatoes to soak into dry country bread, along with roasted fennel, fresh mozzarella, peppery arugula, and bitter radicchio. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, marcella Hazan’s classic tomato sauce proves that great Italian cooking doesn’t need to be complicated. Canned tomatoes simmer gently with butter and onion, creating a rich, silky sauce with remarkable depth and a subtle sweetness. The result is a simple sauce that lets the quality of its few ingredients shine. Get the recipe >.

Breaking: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most key restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most key restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We enhancement this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Latest to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.
